Christian Apologetic Response

Two honest questions, one backward and one forward. Backward: 1 Samuel 15's reprobation of Saul turns on livestock and a spared king — does the punishment fit, or does the narrative deliberately scandalize to establish that partial obedience is disobedience (the chapter's own moral, 15:22-23, 'to obey is better than sacrifice')? Read it as Samuel's theology of kingship (kings don't edit divine commands), not as bloodlust, and say why that reading is textually preferable.

Forward: Amalek-as-archetype (unprovoked attack on stragglers — the weakest) is a moral category Christians need too (who are today's stragglers-attackers, and what does 'blot out' mean when the sword is forbidden us — Matthew 26:52?). The Christian transposition is spiritual and institutional (church discipline, just law, never holy war) — press the transposition question mutually: how does each tradition keep Amalek-memory morally alive without license to kill? Judaism's legal dormancy + liturgical memory is an answer worth learning from, not just critiquing.

Points for Respectful Discussion

Treat Amalek invocations in current-affairs debate with extreme care — real atrocities (October 7 and Gaza both) make abstraction feel obscene, and proof-texting either side's warfare from these verses repeats the instrumentalization both traditions should now renounce. Discuss the category; refuse to deputize it.

Further Resources

  • My Jewish Learning — 'Amalek and the Command to Remember'
  • 1 Samuel 15 — text and commentary (BibleGateway)

Q17What did the Torah's slavery laws actually say — regulation or endorsement?

Context

Exodus 21, Leviticus 25, and Deuteronomy 15 legislate slavery in detail: Hebrew debt-servants serve six years and go free in the seventh (Exodus 21:2; Deuteronomy 15:12-18, with liberation gifts — 'furnish him liberally'), injury frees immediately (eye/tooth, Exodus 21:26-27), killing a slave is punished (21:20-21, however debated), while foreign slaves could be held permanently (Leviticus 25:44-46) — the passage critics cite as endorsement and apologists must face squarely. Runaway slaves must not be returned (Deuteronomy 23:15-16 — unique in the ancient world, directly subversive of the institution).

Mainstream Position & Primary Sources

  • Jewish interpretation: the laws humanize within a universal ancient institution (compare Hammurabi's harsher codes); the Exodus memory ('remember you were slaves in Egypt,' Deuteronomy 15:15) is cited as the laws' moral engine; rabbinic law further softened practice (Ketubot 96a — buying a slave is buying a master, given equality-of-living standards; Maimonides, Slaves 9:8, on humane treatment). Modern Jewish thought (e.g., Heschel, Greenberg) reads the trajectory as liberationist — Torah plants the Exodus dynamic that eventually abolishes.
  • Critical assessment: Leviticus 25:44-46's permanent foreign slavery is real and harsh; harmonizing it fully requires the trajectory hermeneutic (Webb's 'redemptive-movement': Scripture improves on culture and points beyond itself) rather than pretending it reads like 1865. Honest conservatives (Copan, Walton) concede the tension while arguing ANE context (debt, war-captivity, no prisons/welfare) made abolition-talk anachronistic — regulation-toward-humanization was the available good.
  • The New Testament parallel (Philemon; 1 Timothy 1:10's slave-traders condemned; Galatians 3:28) continues the trajectory without yet commanding abolition — the same structure as Torah, advanced one stage (see Islam Q12's comparison).

Primary Source References

  • Exodus 21:1-11, 20-27; Leviticus 25:39-55; Deuteronomy 15:12-18; 23:15-16.
  • Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Slaves 9:8; Babylonian Talmud, Kiddushin 20a.

Christian Apologetic Response

Deploy the trajectory argument symmetrically or not at all: if Torah's slave-laws point beyond themselves (Exodus memory → Jubilee release → runaway protection → Paul's 'no longer as a slave,' Philemon 16), then the Christian must grant Islam's parallel claim (gradualism toward abolition, Islam Q12) a fair hearing too — trajectories are trajectories. The Christian distinctiveness claim is narrower and stronger: only the gospel supplies the mechanism (union with Christ dissolving status — Galatians 3:28; the cross leveling master and slave before one Judge — Ephesians 6:9), not merely the direction.

And confess the church's lag loudly: American slavery's biblical defenders force humility on every use of this question. The trajectory hermeneutic convicts Christians first (why did it take eighteen centuries?) — say that before asking what Torah's Jubilee logic demands of anyone today (debt, trafficking, prison labor — the live applications).

Points for Respectful Discussion

Never quote Leviticus 25:44-46 as a standalone indictment without Exodus 21, Deuteronomy 15 and 23 in the same breath — selective citation is exactly what this book condemns in handling Qur'anic verses (Islam Q8), and Jewish partners will (rightly) return the favor. Whole-canon or silence.

Further Resources

  • My Jewish Learning — 'Slavery in the Torah'
  • William Webb, Slaves, Women & Homosexuals (IVP — redemptive-movement hermeneutic)

Q18Did the Torah really execute people for Sabbath-breaking and adultery?

Context

The Torah prescribes death for a startling catalog: murder (Exodus 21:12), adultery (Leviticus 20:10), blasphemy (24:16), Sabbath violation (Exodus 31:14), idolatry, witchcraft (Exodus 22:18), homosexual acts (Leviticus 20:13), striking parents (Exodus 21:15), and more. The shock is textual and real; the practice, by the tradition's own record, was vanishingly rare. Mishnah Makkot 1:10: a Sanhedrin executing once in seven (or seventy) years is 'murderous' (chovlanit) — Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Tarfon add they'd never have voted death; Rabban Shimon ben Gamaliel retorts they'd then multiply murderers — preserving the debate, characteristically, rather than resolving it.

Mainstream Position & Primary Sources

  • Rabbinic procedure made execution nearly impossible: two valid witnesses, prior warning (hatra'ah) with the offender acknowledging it, Sanhedrin of 23, disqualification of circumstantial evidence ('no conviction without direct testimony'), and majority rules that paradoxically acquit on unanimous guilty votes (a court that unanimously convicts is suspect — Sanhedrin 17a). After 70 CE (and effectively from 30 CE, Sanhedrin 41a — capital jurisdiction withdrawn), executions ceased entirely; the laws became study-texts for moral gravity, not practice.
  • Historical Jesus-context: the woman caught in adultery (John 7:53-8:11, textually disputed but thematically coherent) and Stephen's lynching (Acts 7 — mob action, not Sanhedrin procedure) fit a system where Romans held the sword (John 18:31) and Jewish courts had lost capital power. The Torah's penalties thus functioned in Jesus' day much as now: canonical, unperformed, theologically freighted.
  • Modern Jewish movements: Orthodox retains theoretical validity (awaiting Sanhedrin restoration); Conservative/Reform treat the penalties as historically conditioned; all condemn vigilante enforcement absolutely.

Primary Source References

  • Leviticus 20; Deuteronomy 17:2-7; 19:15-21 (evidentiary law).
  • Mishnah Makkot 1:10; Sanhedrin 41a; John 18:31.

Christian Apologetic Response

The key comparative insight: Judaism defanged its own death-penalty texts through procedure while retaining them canonically — exactly parallel to how Christianity handles herem (Q15: bounded, non-operative) and how Islam debates hudud applicability. Every tradition has a 'severe text, restrained practice' structure; map them together before critiquing any one. Then ask the Christian specificity: the woman-taken-in-adultery pericope (however textually uncertain) captures Jesus' move — neither condoning ('go and sin no more') nor executing ('let him without sin cast first') — mercy and moral seriousness held together, which is structurally what the rabbis attempted procedurally. Is that convergence accident or trajectory?

On homosexuality-capital texts (Leviticus 20:13) specifically: Christians must distinguish decriminalization (affirmed — the church doesn't seek Levitical penalties; Romans 13's sword is the state's, for its own reasons) from moral approval (withheld — Romans 1 stands). The Torah-penalty question is thus separable from the moral question, and conflating them confuses both Jewish and Christian partners. Keep the two tracks explicit.

Points for Respectful Discussion

Present Makkot 1:10's 'murderous court' line with admiration — it is among the tradition's glories, and Christians need its lesson (church history's executions are our shame). Never cite Torah penalties as proof of Jewish harshness; the rabbis' procedural mercy predates Christianity and embarrasses every later religious court, Christian ones included.

Further Resources

  • My Jewish Learning — 'Capital Punishment in Jewish Law'
  • Sefaria — Mishnah Makkot, Chapter 1

Q19Did Israel ever stone a 'stubborn and rebellious son'?

Context

Deuteronomy 21:18-21 prescribes stoning for the ben sorer u-moreh — a gluttonous, drunken son unresponsive to discipline, prosecuted by his own parents before the elders. The Talmud (Sanhedrin 71a) famously concludes: 'There never was and never will be a stubborn and rebellious son' — the law was written, in one view, 'that you may study it and receive reward' (doresh v'kabel sakhar). Conditions pile impossibly: both parents must agree, be physically unimpaired and vocally identical, the son must be within a three-month window after puberty, steal specifically parental meat-and-wine money, and eat it publicly — a legal unicorn.

Mainstream Position & Primary Sources

  • Why preserve an unperformable law? Rabbinic answers: deterrence (the procedure's terror reforms), pedagogy (parental authority's gravity), and theology (some add the son is judged 'for what he will become' — executed for his inevitable murderous future, Sanhedrin 72a's rodef logic extended). Modern scholars add: ANE law collections (Hammurabi, Eshnunna) contain unenforced ideal-statutes; Torah participates in the genre while moralizing it.
  • Jesus' parable of the prodigal (Luke 15) — a gluttonous, rebellious son met by a running father, not elders with stones — reads as deliberate counterpoint whether or not intentionally: grace doing what the unenforceable statute couldn't. And Hebrews 12's discipline-theology ('God disciplines every son') reframes parental severity redemptively.
  • Critics cite the passage as divine endorsement of filicide; defenders cite Sanhedrin 71a as proof the tradition neutered it. Both are half-right: the text's severity is real, and so is the neutralization — the phenomenon to explain is the pairing itself.

Primary Source References

  • Deuteronomy 21:18-21; Proverbs on discipline (13:24; 23:13-14).
  • Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 68b-72a; Luke 15:11-32.

Christian Apologetic Response

Use this as the limiting case for the whole 'severe Torah texts' cluster (Q15-18): here even the rabbis concede non-performance as the text's intent ('study and receive reward'). If Torah itself contains pedagogical-unperformable law by rabbinic admission, then (a) critics can't treat every statute as practiced policy, and (b) traditionalists can't treat every statute as timeless policy either — both sides need a theory of which laws bind how, which is exactly what halakha and (differently) New Testament fulfillment supply. The ben sorer is everyone's tutor in hermeneutics.

The gospel bridge is the prodigal: Torah's rebellious son dies hypothetically; Jesus' rebellious son lives actually, embraced before confession finishes (Luke 15:20-22). Ask whether the parable's father violates Deuteronomy or fulfills its intent (parental love achieving what stones couldn't) — and whether that fulfillment-pattern (law's aim achieved by grace) doesn't unlock the whole Torah. It's a parable-shaped argument for fulfillment; let it work parabolically, not syllogistically.

Points for Respectful Discussion

Read Sanhedrin 71a's impossible conditions aloud with delight — Jewish partners love this sugya, and shared laughter at legal unicorns builds more trust than any argument. Never use the passage to paint Torah as child-killing; the tradition's own verdict ('never was and never will be') is the last word on practice, whatever one makes of the text.

Further Resources

  • Sefaria — Sanhedrin 71a (stubborn and rebellious son)
  • Luke 15 — the Prodigal Son (BibleGateway)

Q20What does Leviticus actually prohibit — and how should Christians handle it today?

Context

Leviticus 18:22 ('mishkevei ishah' — 'lyings of a woman') and 20:13 prohibit male same-sex intercourse, the latter capitally (see Q18's procedural neutering), within the Holiness Code's sexual boundaries (incest, adultery, bestiality, child sacrifice adjacent). The Hebrew's precise scope is debated (all male-male acts? pederasty? cultic? — scholars divide; traditional Judaism reads comprehensively), but the prohibition's presence in both Torah and rabbinic law (Mishneh Torah, Issurei Biah) is undisputed, as is modern Judaism's spectrum: Orthodox retention, Conservative's 2006 responsa permitting (with limits), Reform/Reconstructionist full affirmation.

Mainstream Position & Primary Sources

  • Traditional reading (Orthodox, and historic Christianity): comprehensive prohibition of homosexual acts, reaffirmed in the New Testament (Romans 1:26-27; 1 Corinthians 6:9-10; 1 Timothy 1:10) — making this one of the few Torah sexual ethics explicitly carried into the church, hence non-abrogable by appeal to fulfillment. Defenses of continuity cite the creation-grounding both testaments share (Genesis 1-2 cited by Jesus, Matthew 19:4-6, and Paul, Romans 1).
  • Revisionist readings (Brownson, Vines, some mainline scholars): the texts target exploitation (pederasty, prostitution, excess passion — Romans 1's 'exchanged' logic), not covenanted same-sex unions unknown to antiquity; 'arsenokoites' (1 Corinthians 6:9) is obscure enough to dispute. Traditionalists reply that Leviticus' placement among categorical prohibitions (not case-laws) and Romans 1's nature-language resist reduction to exploitation.
  • Pastoral reality both sides face: real people, real suffering, church/synagogue wounds, youth suicide risks — the debate's human cost exceeds its exegetical stakes in every congregation.

Primary Source References

  • Leviticus 18:22; 20:13; Genesis 1-2; Matthew 19:4-6.
  • Romans 1:26-27; 1 Corinthians 6:9-11; Mishneh Torah, Issurei Biah 21.

Christian Apologetic Response

Christians must hold three things at once, and this question tests whether we can: (1) the moral judgment stands (the revisionist case, however sincerely argued, must overcome both testaments' plain sense — say so without caricaturing its best scholars); (2) the penalty emphatically does not transfer (Q18's procedural mercy + John 8's non-condemnation + Romans 13's limited sword = no Christian case for criminalization of private acts, and the church's punitive history here is confessed sin); (3) the pastoral posture is embrace-without-affirmation modeled on Jesus with tax collectors (table fellowship preceding transformation, Luke 19) and Paul's 'such were some of you... washed' (1 Corinthians 6:11 — identity in Christ, not orientation, as the final word).

With Jewish partners, note the shared structure (prohibition retained, penalty dropped, pastoral agony shared) and ask the Messianic-era question both traditions must face: if the age to come heals all brokenness (Isaiah 35; Revelation 21), what does faithfulness look like meanwhile for those whose experience doesn't change — celibacy's dignity (honored in both traditions' saints), community's embrace, hope's patience? End in pastoral solidarity, not culture war. The tone of this entry is the argument.

Points for Respectful Discussion

This entry must be pastorally impeccable: no slurs, no jokes, no speculation about individuals, no ranking this sin above greed or divorce (the church's selective ferocity here is its shame — Matthew 7:3-5 first). Affirm LGBTQ persons' full human dignity and the church's duty of radical welcome (everyone belongs before anyone believes), while stating the historic sexual ethic without apology. Both firmness and tenderness are non-negotiable; if you can only do one, don't raise the topic.

Further Resources

  • My Jewish Learning — 'Homosexuality in Jewish Law' (spectrum overview)
  • Rosaria Butterfield / Wesley Hill — celibacy-and-grace pastoral voices (publisher pages)

Q21What was women's status under Torah law — oppressed or protected?

Context

The Torah's gender texts cut both ways, and honest apologetics reports both edges: patrilineal inheritance (daughters inherit only without sons — until Zelophehad's daughters win reform, Numbers 27:1-11; 36), levirate marriage (Deuteronomy 25:5-10), the sotah ordeal for suspected adultery (Numbers 5:11-31 — the woman drinks, the man doesn't), vow-annulment by fathers/husbands (Numbers 30), menstrual separation (Leviticus 15:19-30), bride-price and virginity laws (Exodus 22:16-17; Deuteronomy 22), male-only priesthood and (mostly) male legal testimony — alongside counter-texts: Deborah judges Israel (Judges 4-5), Huldah authenticates Scripture (2 Kings 22), women prophesy (Exodus 15:20; Joel 2:28), inherit (Zelophehad), vow directly (Hannah, 1 Samuel 1), and own property (Proverbs 31).

Mainstream Position & Primary Sources

  • Traditional Judaism: the structure reflects creational/functional differentiation, not inferiority — women's exemption from time-bound positive mitzvot frees for higher obligations (family), and aggadah overflows with matriarchal honor (Sarah's prophecy exceeding Abraham's, Rosh Hashanah 16b; 'a man must honor his wife more than himself,' Yevamot 62b; the eshet chayil as Torah-embodied). Feminist critics (Plaskow, Adler) reply that honor-language coexisted with real legal disability, and modern movements have reformed accordingly (women rabbis since 1972 Reform/1985 Conservative; Orthodox partnership minyan debates ongoing).
  • Ancient Near Eastern comparison favors Torah relatively: Middle Assyrian laws (veiling mandates, impalement for abortion, wife-mutilation for husband's crimes) and Hammurabi's vicarious punishments (builder's daughter executed for collapse) exceed Torah's restraints; Deuteronomy 24:16 ('fathers shall not be put to death for children') repudiates vicarious punishment explicitly. Relative-to-context vs. absolute-standard is the whole methodological fight.
  • Jesus' record (Luke 8:1-3 women funders; John 4 theological dialogue; resurrection commission, John 20:17-18; Galatians 3:28) elevates within Judaism's world — best read as prophetic intensification of Torah's own counter-texts, not pagan import.

Primary Source References

  • Numbers 5:11-31 (sotah); 27:1-11 (Zelophehad); Deuteronomy 22; 24:1-4, 16.
  • Judges 4-5; 2 Kings 22:14-20; Luke 8:1-3; John 20:11-18.

Christian Apologetic Response

Argue comparatively and redemptively: Torah improved its world (compare Assyria honestly) while encoding its world's patriarchy (concede honestly) — the trajectory question again (Q17's redemptive-movement hermeneutic). Then the Christian claim: Jesus treats women as theological interlocutors and resurrection witnesses (in a culture barring female testimony — Celsus mocked the resurrection on exactly this ground, and the church kept the embarrassing detail, an authenticity marker worth pressing everywhere), and Pentecost universalizes Joel's daughters-prophesying (Acts 2:17-18). The arc from Zelophehad to Mary Magdalene is one story; tell it whole.

With Muslim partners (Islam's testimony/inheritance/hijab debates), this entry models method: concede your text's hard edges (sotah asymmetry), contextualize without excusing, and trace reform from inside (Huldah → Jesus → Galatians 3:28). Whatever standard you apply to Qur'an 4:34/2:282, apply here first — the book's credibility depends on it.

Points for Respectful Discussion

Never pit 'Christianity liberated women' against 'Judaism oppressed them' — the claim is historically false (rabbinic honor-texts are real; Christian patriarchal abuses are real) and pastorally toxic. The honest frame is shared struggle toward founding ideals, with Jesus as the intensifier both traditions must reckon with. Read Phyllis Trible and Richard Bauckham's Gospel Women before debating this.

Further Resources

  • My Jewish Learning — 'Women in the Bible' (overview)
  • Richard Bauckham, Gospel Women (Eerdmans overview)

Q22Why did the patriarchs practice polygamy if marriage is one-man-one-woman?

Context

Abraham (Hagar, Keturah), Jacob (Leah, Rachel, Bilhah, Zilpah), Gideon, David (multiple wives), Solomon (700 wives, 300 concubines — 1 Kings 11:3) — the narrative record is undeniable, and critics (Muslim apologists defending Muhammad's marriages, Islam Q2; secularists charging inconsistency) press it. The Torah regulates polygamy (Exodus 21:10-11 — maintenance rights; Deuteronomy 21:15-17 — firstborn protection; Leviticus 18:18 — no sister-rivals) without ever commanding it, while Genesis 1-2 establishes the creation pattern ('a man... united to his wife, and they become one flesh,' 2:24) that Jesus later absolutizes (Matthew 19:4-9; Mark 10:5-9 — 'because of hardness of heart,' divorce and, by extension, polygamy as concession).

Mainstream Position & Primary Sources

  • Jewish handling: the patriarchs' marriages are narrated with their miseries foregrounded (Sarah vs. Hagar — Genesis 16, 21; Leah vs. Rachel — Genesis 29-30; Hannah vs. Peninnah — 1 Samuel 1) — the text's own polemic against the practice. Rabbinic law permitted polygamy until Rabbenu Gershom's ban (c. 1000 CE, Ashkenaz; Sephardim followed effectively, Yemenites latest) — desuetude, not repudiation. Deuteronomy 17:17's king-law ('he shall not multiply wives') judges Solomon explicitly (1 Kings 11's verdict: wives 'turned his heart').
  • Christian handling: creation-pattern + concession-framework (Matthew 19) — God regulated what He didn't institute, then restored the pattern in Christ (Ephesians 5:25-33 — one husband, one bride, imaging Christ-Church). The pastorals require monogamy of leaders (1 Timothy 3:2) as the church's beachhead. Islam's four-wife cap with justice-condition (Qur'an 4:3, Islam Q2) represents a third model: permanent regulation — compare the three models directly (concession-to-restoration vs. permanent-cap).

Primary Source References

  • Genesis 2:24; 16; 29-30; Deuteronomy 17:17; 21:15-17; 1 Kings 11:1-13.
  • Matthew 19:3-9; Ephesians 5:25-33; Rabbenu Gershom's ban (historical overviews).

Christian Apologetic Response

The comparative triptych is the payoff: Judaism (narrated misery → millennial desuetude → ban), Christianity (creation pattern → hardness concession → Christ-restoration), Islam (cap + justice-condition, permanent). Ask which model best fits the data: the Bible's polygamy stories read as cautionary (every one ends in tears — make the partner name an exception; there isn't one), suggesting the text subverts what it records. That's a literary observation available to all, and it favors restoration-models over permanent-regulation ones.

With Muslim partners specifically: Muhammad's exemption (33:50, Islam Q2) plus permanent four-wife permission vs. Jesus' return to Genesis 2:24 — which prophet restores creation, and which accommodates it? Frame as lawgiver-ethics (the question Islam Q2 poses), not as Western moralizing (serial monogamy and pornified divorce-culture forfeit the high ground — confess it). The argument is canonical, not cultural.

Points for Respectful Discussion

Read the misery-texts closely (Hagar's wilderness theophany — Genesis 16:13, the only person in Scripture to name God — is among the Bible's tenderest passages) and let them do the work; hammering polygamists while ignoring Christian divorce rates is the hypocrisy that kills this question. Canon first, culture second, self-critique always.

Further Resources

  • Gordon Wenham, Story as Torah (Baker — narrative ethics method)
  • Matthew 19 — divorce/remarriage text (BibleGateway)

Q23What were the purity laws for — hygiene, holiness, or misogyny?

Context

Leviticus 12-15 and Numbers 19 construct an elaborate purity system: childbirth impurity (12), skin disease (tzara'at, 13-14), genital discharges (15), menstrual separation (niddah, 15:19-30; 18:19), corpse impurity (Numbers 19, red heifer rite) — with mikveh immersion as restoration. Mary Douglas (Purity and Danger; Leviticus as Literature) reframed the system: impurity maps disorder/death (blood = life lost, corpses = death itself, scale-disease = living decay), so purity disciplines Israel to embody God's life-order — holiness as wholeness, not hygiene (the system predates germ theory by millennia and includes non-contagious states).

Mainstream Position & Primary Sources

  • Jewish practice: niddah (monthly separation + mikveh) remains widely observed even among the Modern Orthodox and many traditionalists as marriage-sanctifying discipline (taharat ha-mishpacha literature frames it positively: cyclical renewal, restraint eroticizing reunion); corpse-impurity laws are dormant without red heifer/Temple (a live Third-Temple flashpoint — red heifer candidates in Israel make news); kashrut-adjacent handwashing (netilat yadayim) structures daily life. Feminist critics (Wasserfall, Adler) charge niddah encodes female-bodily shame; defenders cite women's own testimony of meaning and the system's symmetry (male discharges equally defiling — Leviticus 15 covers both).
  • Jesus' purity confrontations: touching lepers (Mark 1:41 — compassion overriding quarantine logic), the bleeding woman (Mark 5:25-34 — her touch doesn't defile Him; His power heals her: purity flows outward, reversing the system), corpse-touching (Jairus's daughter, Luke 8:54), and the programmatic declaration (Mark 7:15 — defilement from within). Hebrews 9-10 theologizes: conscience-cleansing by blood of Christ replaces ritual washings ('dead works').

Primary Source References

  • Leviticus 12; 15; Numbers 19; Leviticus 11-15 structure.
  • Mark 1:40-45; 5:25-34; 7:14-23; Hebrews 9:11-14.

Christian Apologetic Response

The Douglas insight is the apologetic key: if impurity = death-signs quarantined from God's life-presence, then Jesus touching lepers/corpses/bleeders isn't laxity but invasion — Life entering the quarantine zone. The bleeding woman's healing (power 'going out,' Mark 5:30) dramatizes fulfillment: what mikveh symbolized (restoration to life-order), Christ effects. Ask the partner to read Mark 5 with Leviticus 15 open — the intertextuality is so precise (twelve years, 'flow of blood' language) that literary accident is implausible; the evangelist knew exactly which purity law he was fulfilling.

On niddah-as-misogyny specifically: concede the feminist critique's force where practice shames (some communal implementations do), distinguish text from implementation (Leviticus 15's male-female symmetry complicates the charge), and note Christianity's parallel struggle (historical churching-of-women rites, menstruation taboos in some traditions). Shared texts, shared distortions, shared reform — argue the trajectory (life-order fulfilled in resurrection-life, Romans 6:4) rather than impugning motives.

Points for Respectful Discussion

Read Douglas before debating purity — without her, Christians default to 'weird primitive hygiene' condescension that misreads the system and insults its keepers. And never weaponize niddah against Orthodox women, many of whom observe it devoutly and articulate its meaning better than any critic; descriptive respect precedes normative debate, always.

Further Resources

  • Mary Douglas, Purity and Danger (Routledge)
  • My Jewish Learning — 'Taharat HaMishpacha (Family Purity)'

Q24Who were the Pharisees, Sadducees, and Essenes — and which one did Jesus resemble?

Context

Second Temple Judaism (516 BCE-70 CE) was no monolith: Sadducees (aristocratic priestly elite, Temple-centered, Torah-only authority rejecting resurrection/angels — Acts 23:8; Josephus; disappeared with the Temple), Pharisees (lay-scholar movement, Oral Torah + resurrection + providence-and-freedom synthesis; ancestors of Rabbinic Judaism; Josephus counts 6,000), Essenes (separatist purity communes, plausibly the Qumran/Dead Sea Scrolls community — celibate, solar calendar, apocalyptic dualism), plus Zealots, Herodians, Samaritans, and the am ha'aretz (common folk). The Gospels' conflicts assume this map; without it, 'the Jews' flattens into caricature.

Mainstream Position & Primary Sources

  • Josephus (Jewish War, Antiquities) is the primary describer, with the Scrolls (Community Rule, Damascus Document, War Scroll) voicing Essene-type sectarianism firsthand and the New Testament supplying Pharisaic/Sadducean encounters. Rabbinic literature retrojects, calling pre-70 sages 'Pharisees' loosely (Hillel/Shammai schools). Modern scholarship (Sanders, Neusner, Schiffman) warns against Gospel-mirror-reading: 'Pharisee' in Matthew often means post-70 rabbinic opponents retrojected, and pre-70 Pharisaism was popular and pious, not a byword for hypocrisy.
  • Jesus' alignments: resurrection + angels + Oral-tradition engagement (corban debate assumes the category) = broadly Pharisaic theology; Temple-action + woe-oracles + table-fellowship with sinners = prophetic critique of all parties; divorce strictness (Matthew 19) sides Hillel-vs-Shammai specifically (the 'any matter' clause = Hillel's leniency, which Jesus rejects for Shammai-like strictness — a detail proving insider fluency). Paul's self-description ('a Pharisee, son of Pharisees,' Acts 23:6; Philippians 3:5) clinches Christianity's Pharisaic roots.
  • The ' Essene-Jesus' thesis (Jesus as Essene, or John the Baptist as one) persists popularly (Baigent/Leigh-era sensationalism) but lacks evidence: Jesus' wine-drinking, sinner-fellowship, and Temple-engagement invert Qumran separatism point by point.

Primary Source References

  • Josephus, Antiquities 13, 18; Jewish War 2 (parties).
  • Acts 23:6-10; Matthew 23 (woes in context); Dead Sea Scrolls, Community Rule (1QS).

Christian Apologetic Response

The payoff is demolishing two mirror-image libels: the Christian caricature (Pharisees = legalistic hypocrites — refuted by Paul's pride in Pharisaism and the movement's genuine piety) and the polemical counter (Jesus = Essene drop-out or pagan import — refuted by His Pharisaic theology + prophetic critique pattern). The historical Jesus was a Torah-observant Jew debating fellow Jews intra-murally — say this plainly and watch both antisemitic supersessionism and mythicist nonsense lose their footing simultaneously.

Then the fork both sides must face: if Jesus was (as Sanders's 'historical Jesus' consensus grants) a first-century Jew announcing God's kingdom with unprecedented authority (forgiving sins, Mark 2:7; judging Temple, Mark 11-13), the intra-Jewish debate of 30 CE became the world-historical schism of 90 CE (Birkat ha-Minim, Yavneh) — so when, exactly, did the ways part, and was the parting about Torah (which Jewish Christians kept for generations) or about Jesus' person (which is what the sources actually argue about)? Force the question onto christology, where it belongs, by conceding everything historical first.

Points for Respectful Discussion

Never use 'Pharisee' as an insult — not in sermons, not in debate. It is a living tradition's ancestors you're slurring (modern rabbis are Pharisees' heirs), and every such slur confirms Jewish suspicions about Christian motives. Say 'some Pharisees Jesus debated' with the same specificity you'd demand ('some Christians,' never 'Christians') — reciprocity is the method.

Further Resources

  • E.P. Sanders, Jesus and Judaism (Fortress — the landmark)
  • Dead Sea Scrolls digital library (Qumran texts)

Q25Where did the synagogue come from — and why does church look like it?

Context

The synagogue (proseuche/bet knesset) — prayer, Scripture reading, and sermon without sacrifice — has no Torah mandate and murky origins: traditionally exilic (Ezekiel's 'small sanctuary,' 11:16; Psalm 137's rivers of Babylon), archaeologically visible from the 3rd century BCE (Egyptian inscriptions, Delos, later Gamla/Masada/Magdala halls), and ubiquitous by Jesus' day (Nazareth, Capernaum — Mark 1:21; Luke 4:16-30's lectionary-like reading). It was Second Temple Judaism's adaptive genius: worship survivable without Temple — the institution that made post-70 survival (and Q8's atonement-substitution) possible.

Mainstream Position & Primary Sources

  • Scholarly consensus (Levine, Binder, Runesson): synagogues were multi-use community halls (court, school, hostel, prayer) before specializing liturgically; the Theodotus inscription (pre-70 Jerusalem) lists Torah reading and study as core functions. After 70, Yavneh centered the synagogue-liturgical system (amidah, Torah service) that defines Judaism since — an innovation of staggering success, whatever one's theology of it.
  • The church's debt is structural and obvious: Sunday/weekly assembly, Scripture readings + homily, psalmody, prayers, elders/overseers (paralleling zekenim/parnasim), even architecture (basilica-bema layouts). Earliest Christians met in synagogues (Acts' missionary pattern) until expulsion (John 9:22; Birkat ha-Minim c. 90 CE), then replicated the form with christological content. Supersessionist narratives of church-as-novelty collapse on this evidence — and honest Christians should be the first to say so.
  • Liturgy parallels run deep: the amidah's blessings and the Lord's Prayer share petitionary DNA (kaddish's 'magnified and sanctified be His great name' ≈ 'hallowed be thy name'); Sabbath lectionary cycles prefigure the church's lectionaries.

Primary Source References

  • Ezekiel 11:16; Psalm 137; Luke 4:16-30; Acts 13:13-43; 17:1-4.
  • Theodotus inscription; Lee Levine, The Ancient Synagogue (Yale).

Christian Apologetic Response

The appreciative argument first: synagogue is proof of Judaism's theological resilience — worship without altar, community without Temple, hope without sovereignty — and Christianity inherited the form so completely that every Sunday service is an unacknowledged tribute. Say that; mean it. Then the developmental question both traditions answer differently: synagogue adapted to Temple-loss by substitution (Q8), church adapted to Temple-loss by fulfillment-claim (Christ as Temple, John 2:19-21, claimed before 70). Same catastrophe, same decade, two theories — which better explains the first Christians' non-anxiety (Hebrews written pre-70, already relativizing the cult)?

Press the Birkat ha-Minim dating gently (Yavneh's 'blessing' against heretics, twelfth benediction, c. 85-90 CE — the institutional parting): the split postdates Jesus by sixty years and centers on christology (confessing Jesus), not Torah (Jewish Christians kept it). So the synagogue/church fork is evidence for, not against, the claim that Jesus' person — not ritual or ethics — was always the issue. Let institutional history carry the christological conclusion; it's harder to dismiss than prooftexts.

Points for Respectful Discussion

Visit synagogues when invited (Shabbat morning Torah service is profoundly moving), follow the stand/sit cues, wear the kippah offered, and never treat the liturgy as a missionary prop — presence without agenda is itself the apologetic. And retire 'synagogue of Satan' (Revelation 2:9) from all casual use; its original referent (specific persecutors in Smyrna/Philadelphia) never licensed general application, and its misuse history is soaked in blood.

Further Resources

  • Lee Levine, The Ancient Synagogue (Yale UP overview)
  • My Jewish Learning — 'The Synagogue Through History'

Q26Is Genesis 3:15 a messianic prophecy — the 'first gospel'?

Context

Genesis 3:15 ('I will put enmity between you and the woman, between your seed and her seed; he shall bruise your head, and you shall bruise his heel') — the protevangelium — stands at the canon's head: judgment-oracle on the serpent containing aEmbedded hope. The oddities drive the debate: 'her seed' (seed traced through the woman — anomalous in patrilineal Scripture), the masculine singular pronoun (hu' — 'HE shall bruise,' individual, not collective), and the asymmetric wounds (heel bruised, head crushed — suffering plus victory). Jewish reading: ongoing human-serpent enmity (peshat: snakes and people; midrashic: humanity's struggle with evil; Targum Onkelos reads Messiah's days into it partially — 'they will... in the days of King Messiah'!). Christian reading (Irenaeus onward; Galatians 4:4 — 'born of woman'; Romans 16:20 — God crushing Satan; Revelation 12 — woman, child, dragon): the verse's grammar demands an individual, virginally-significant ('her seed'), suffering-victorious deliverer.

Mainstream Position & Primary Sources

  • Jewish (Rashi: serpent vs. humanity; Ibn Ezra similar; modern critical: etiology of snake-fear): the 'seed' is collective posterity both sides; crushing/bruising describe perennial conflict, not eschatology. Partial concessions exist: Targum Pseudo-Jonathan explicitly messianic ('...in the days of the King Messiah'); Zohar reads Messiah here; medieval disputations show Jews knew the Christian claim intimately. Modern Jewish counter-missionary (Singer): singular pronoun is generic ('one will bruise' — Hebrew idiom), 'her seed' unremarkable.
  • Christian: the pronoun's masculinity + singularity + the woman's-seed anomaly + canonical trajectory (Romans 16:20's crushing; Hebrews 2:14's death-destroying-death; 1 John 3:8's Son-destroys-devil's-works) converge — Genesis 3:15 as the acorn of Isaiah 53 and the cross. Patristic unanimity (Justin, Irenaeus, Tertullian) shows the reading is apostolic-era, not medieval invention.

Primary Source References

  • Genesis 3:14-15; Romans 16:20; Galatians 4:4; Revelation 12:1-5.
  • Targum Pseudo-Jonathan on Gen 3:15 (Sefaria).

Christian Apologetic Response

Press the grammar-trio as one interlocking observation: (1) 'her seed' — Scripture traces seed through fathers without exception (Genesis 12:7, 15:5, 17:7 — 'your seed'); the sole maternal-seed phrase in Torah lands here, at the fall, promising the undone-by-woman ('through woman came... ' — Paul completes it: 'born of woman,' Galatians 4:4 — the virgin birth's deep root, deeper than Isaiah 7:14!). (2) hu' — masculine singular; collective readings must dissolve the pronoun the verse sharpens. (3) head/heel asymmetry — mere snake-fights bruise ankles but crush no heads decisively; the verse promises decisive victory THROUGH shared wounding — the cross's exact shape (Colossians 2:15 — triumphing 'by the cross'; heel wounded Friday, head crushed Sunday). Three anomalies, one Fulfillment fitting all three — coincidence strains credulity past breaking.

Add the Targum witness (pre-Christian Jewish Aramaic paraphrase hearing Messiah here!): the messianic reading has Jewish roots — Christians didn't invent it, they inherited and identified it. Then the canonical bookend (Genesis 3:15's promised crusher → Revelation 20:10's crushed dragon in the lake of fire): the Bible's first prophecy and last fulfillment share a serpent, a seed, and a crushing. Ask whether any merely-human book ends its 1,500-year arc answering its third chapter — the Bible's unity is the argument's silent engine.

Points for Respectful Discussion

Present the Hebrew gently (hu', zera' — transliterate; don't perform expertise you lack), concede etiological layers exist (snakes ARE scary — peshat and prophecy coexist in Hebrew narrative habitually), and never claim Genesis 3:15 'proves' the virgin birth alone (it hints; Isaiah 7:14 specifies; Matthew 1 fulfills — the chain, not the link, convinces). Cumulative case, humbly offered, Targum-cited.

Further Resources

  • Genesis 3 — text (BibleGateway)
  • Targum Pseudo-Jonathan Gen 3 (Sefaria)

Q27Through whom are 'all nations blessed' — Israel, or Abraham's Seed?

Context

Genesis 12:3 ('in you all families of the earth shall be blessed' — niphal/hithpael debated: 'shall be blessed' vs. 'shall bless themselves') anchors the Abrahamic covenant, repeated to Isaac (26:4) and Jacob (28:14), narrowed to Judah (49:10), then David (2 Samuel 7). Jewish reading: blessing flows through Israel — Torah's light, ethical monotheism's gift to civilization, proselyte-welcome, and ultimately the messianic age's universal knowledge (Isaiah 2:2-4; Maimonides' universal horizon). Christian reading (Galatians 3:8, 16 — Paul's double move: 'Scripture preached the gospel beforehand to Abraham' + 'seed' (sperma, singular!) as Christ): the promise's grammar is singular-personal, and its fulfillment is the Abrahamic blessing (forgiveness/Spirit) reaching Gentiles through the Jewish Messiah — empirically: billions of Gentiles worshipping Abraham's God today trace it to Jesus, not to proselyte courts.

Mainstream Position & Primary Sources

  • Grammatical flashpoint: Paul's singular-seed argument (Galatians 3:16 — 'not seeds as of many, but as of one... Christ') strikes modern readers as midrashic sleight (collective nouns take singular verbs routinely; Jewish scholars cry foul — Stern?; Sanders notes Paul's creative exegesis). Defenses: Genesis itself oscillates seed-collective/seed-individual (22:17-18 — seed as stars AND as the one through whom blessing comes; the binding-of-Isaac context personalizes!); ancient readers heard both registers; Paul's reading has canonical company (the singular Servant/Seed trajectory through Samuel-Kings to Isaiah).
  • Historical flashpoint: has Israel blessed the nations? Judaism answers yes (monotheism, ethics, Sabbath, Jesus Himself a Jew!). Christianity answers yes-through-Jesus (the nations' blessing is measurable: global worship of YHWH via the church — a historical datum, not a doctrine). Both claim the fruit; the debate is the tree.

Primary Source References

  • Genesis 12:1-3; 22:15-18; Galatians 3:6-16.
  • Isaiah 2:2-4; Maimonides on universal knowledge (MT Kings 12).

Christian Apologetic Response

Grant Israel's civilizational blessing lavishly (alphabet? law? weekend? — the West's furniture is Jewish-made; ingratitude here is obscene, and Christian antisemitism denies the very blessing it enjoys — Romans 11:18's warning: 'you do not support the root'). THEN the singularity-plus-history double punch: (1) Genesis 22's binding personalizes the seed (ONE son offered, ONE ram substitute, blessing pronounced on the Moriah mountain — topography of substitution! — ram for Isaac prefigures Lamb for world, John 1:29); (2) history's audit — two millennia on, which Abrahamic claimant actually gathered 'all families'? Synagogue proselytism (noble, tiny) vs. the church of the nations (2+ billion confessing Abraham's God through Jesus)? The promise's scale demands a fulfillment of matching scale — only the Messiah-movement qualifies empirically. Fruit inspects roots (Matthew 7:16 works on religions too).

Meet Paul's exegesis charge head-on (don't dodge Galatians 3:16's difficulty — acknowledge the collective-singular slide, then show Genesis 22 earns the singular: one heir, one mountain, one substitute). Honesty about Paul's method (midrashic, aggressive, first-century-Jewish — exactly how Qumran and Philo argue!) disarms the 'Paul twisted it' dismissal: he argued like his contemporaries because he WAS one — a Pharisee (Q24-entry!) exegeting Israel's text Israel's way, reaching Jesus. Method respected, conclusion pressed.

Points for Respectful Discussion

Never present Gentile Christianity as replacing Israel in the blessing (Romans 11 forbids it — wild branches grafted, root intact; supersessionism here is exegetical theft — Q94-entry), never minimize proselyte-paths (Ruth the Moabite ancestress of David AND of Christ (Matthew 1:5!) — she's both traditions' 증거... witness), and count the blessing empirically with humility (the church's Gentile millions include centuries of coerced baptisms — forced fruit rots; count willing worship, which still overwhelms).

Further Resources

  • Genesis 12; 22 — texts (BibleGateway)
  • Galatians 3 — seed argument (BibleGateway)

Q28What is 'Shiloh' — and when did Judah's scepter depart?

Context

Genesis 49:10 ('The scepter shall not depart from Judah... until Shiloh comes, and to him shall be the obedience of the peoples') — Jacob's deathbed oracle — is the Torah's first dated messianic clock: tribal sovereignty persists UNTIL a coming figure who draws Gentile obedience. Shiloh's meaning is genuinely uncertain (personal name? 'to whom it belongs' (shai lo — Ezekiel 21:27's 'until he comes to whom it belongs'!)? place-name Shiloh (1 Samuel 1-4's sanctuary — 'until he comes to Shiloh' = pre-monarchic horizon?)? 'his son' (shilo = offspring?)?). Jewish readings split: Targum Onkelos + Talmud (Sanhedrin 98b — 'Shiloh is his [Messiah's] name'!) + Rashi = Messiah (royal line continuing through exilarchs in exile); modern critical = Davidic dynasty's rise (scepter arrives WITH David — 'until' as terminus a quo?) or Josiah. Christian reading: scepter = tribal self-rule (especially capital jurisdiction); it departed at Jesus' advent — Herod the Idumean (non-Judahite!) on the throne, then 70 CE's end; 'obedience of peoples' (Gentiles!) fits only the church age.

Mainstream Position & Primary Sources

  • The capital-power datum both sides must handle: John 18:31 ('It is not lawful for us to put anyone to death') + Talmudic tradition (Sanhedrin 41a — Sanhedrin exiled itself from the Chamber of Hewn Stone forty years before 70, ending capital cases; they lamented 'woe, the scepter has departed from Judah!' — Avodah Zarah 8b / Sanhedrin 41a traditions!). Dated ~30 CE — Jesus' trial decade. The correspondence (scepter departs exactly when Shiloh arrives, per Christian chronology) is either providential or the eeriest coincidence in religious history.
  • Objections: 'peoples' obedience' unfulfilled (worldunconverted — the standard Jewish rejoinder, Q2's framework: first/second coming); scepter as mere tribal identity (survived in exilarchs — Rashi's line); Shiloh-as-place (Shiloh sanctuary era — oracle expires with judges?). Each has weight; none dissolves Sanhedrin 98b's messianic consensus.

Primary Source References

  • Genesis 49:8-12; Ezekiel 21:27; John 18:31.
  • Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 98b (Shiloh = Messiah); 41a (capital power).

Christian Apologetic Response

Lead with the Talmud's double witness (98b: Shiloh IS Messiah — the rabbis' own identification, precluding 'Christian invention' charges; 41a: scepter departed ~30 CE — the rabbis' own dating, coinciding with Jesus' trial to the decade). The combination is lethal to dismissal: your sages named the figure and dated the departure; the Nazarene fills both blanks simultaneously. Press the 41a lament ('woe, the scepter has departed!') beside John 18:31 — the Sanhedrin confessing Genesis 49:10's fulfillment-condition while judging the fulfiller. Irony this precise is either inspiration or indictment.

Then the peoples-test, answered with eschatological patience (Q2's two-comings framework — first coming gathers firstfruits (Gentile church: 'obedience of peoples' begun — Romans 15:18's 'obedience of the Gentiles' uses the exact concept!), second completes). And the exilarch-rejoinder (Rashi's continuing scepter): exilarchs wielded Persian-delegated communal authority, not Judah's scepter (no tribe, no territory, no Torah-jurisdiction over life/death) — scepter means sovereignty, and sovereignty died with Agrippa II (~100 CE) at the latest. Every alternative dating puts Messiah AFTER sovereignty's end — i.e., now-impossible (no tribe survives to identify him!). The oracle's logic forces a first-century Shiloh — or a failed oracle. Choose.

Points for Respectful Discussion

Cite Sanhedrin 98b/41a from Sefaria with tractate precision (bluffing Talmud citations is instantly detected), concede 'peoples' full-obedience awaits consummation (don't claim the church age completes it — Revelation says otherwise), and never use 41a triumphantly ('your own Talmud proves it, ha!') — the rabbis' lament is sacred grief over lost sovereignty; handle it as you would a funeral text (because it is one).

Further Resources

  • Genesis 49 — Jacob's blessing (BibleGateway)
  • Sanhedrin 98b; 41a (Sefaria)

Q29Who is the 'star out of Jacob' — David, Bar Kokhba, or Christ?

Context

Numbers 24:17 (Balaam's fourth oracle: 'a star shall come out of Jacob, and a scepter shall rise out of Israel; it shall crush the forehead of Moab and break down all the sons of Sheth') — star + scepter, royal-destroyer imagery — has three claimants across history: David (2 Samuel 8:2 — Moab measured with lines, executed in thirds — Rashi/Ibn Ezra's peshat; Moab crushed literally), Bar Kokhba (Shimon bar Kosiba, hailed by Rabbi Akiva as Messiah — 'son of the star' (bar kokhba!) — coins stamped with stars, 132-135 CE revolt, catastrophic failure, after which sages renamed him bar Koziba ('son of lies')), and Christ (Matthew 2's magi-star; Revelation 22:16 — 'I am... the bright morning star'). The Bar Kokhba episode is evidentially priceless: it proves pre-Christian Judaism read the verse messianically (Akiva needed no innovation — the reading was traditional).

Mainstream Position & Primary Sources

  • Jewish: David fulfilled it (Moab crushed — done, history closed; messianic reuse is midrashic surplus). Christian: David partially (Moab ≠ 'all sons of Sheth' — universal language exceeds the peshat; the oracle's cosmic scope ('ends of the earth' context, 24:14 'latter days'!) demands eschatological fulfillment; Matthew 2's star (Gentile astrologers guided by Jewish prophecy — the nations coming to the light, Isaiah 60:3!) plus Revelation 22:16's self-identification close the loop. Critical: Balaam-oracles as monarchic propaganda (Davidic court projecting backward — minimalists; the Moab specificity anchors 10th-century politics).
  • Bar Kokhba's reuse cuts both ways and must be handled with care: it proves messianic reading (good for Christians) but also proves messianic readings fail (good for skeptics — Akiva was wrong; why not the apostles?). The distinguishing test both sides accept: Bar Kokhba died and stayed dead (Koziba!); resurrection is Christianity's differentiator (1 Corinthians 15:14's falsifiability — Judaism and Christianity agree dead messiahs aren't messiahs!).

Primary Source References

  • Numbers 24:14-19; 2 Samuel 8:2; Matthew 2:1-12; Revelation 22:16.
  • Bar Kokhba coins/revolt (archaeological/historical overviews).

Christian Apologetic Response

Argue fulfillment-escalation (peshat + surplus, not peshat versus surplus): David truly crushed Moab (grant the history — 2 Samuel 8's lines-and-execution is brutal fact), yet 'all sons of Sheth' (all humanity's chaos, Seth = mankind's root!) and 'latter days' (24:14) overflow David's horizon — prophecy's near/far pattern (with Isaiah 7:14-entry J3: sign-child then, Immanuel ultimately). Then the magi masterstroke: pagan astrologers, reading a Jewish oracle's star, bring Gentile gold to a Jewish infant — 'obedience of peoples' (Genesis 49:10, previous entry!) enacted in swaddling clothes. The nations' first worship precedes Israel's rejection (Matthew 2:3 — Herod 'troubled, and all Jerusalem with him' — the pattern of the whole gospel in one verse!). Ask: who arranged Gentile stargazers to fulfill Torah-oracles if not Torah's God?

On Bar Kokhba: concede Akiva's error fully (great rabbis err — Akiva's martyrdom (Yom Kippur liturgy's Eleh Ezkerah!) doesn't validate his messianism; error is error), then press resurrection as the control both traditions honor (Maimonides' own principle: a failed/killed claimant is excluded (Kings 11:4 — Jesus AND Bar Kokhba both fail the survival test on strictly Maimonidean grounds... unless resurrection (the apostles' claim, attested (Q7-entry!) — Maimonides never examined the resurrection evidence; invite the examination (1 Corinthians 15:3-8's 500, tombs, transformations — historical, not dogmatic). Bar Kokhba died; the question is whether Jesus stayed dead. Everything turns there — as Paul himself insisted.

Points for Respectful Discussion

Honor Akiva's martyrdom separately from his messianism (Romans died him for Torah — Eleh Ezkerah's flayed-flesh Shema is among Judaism's holiest memories; sneering at Akiva over Bar Kokhba profanes martyrdom), present the magi with historical sobriety (Parthian magi? Babylonian Jews' Daniel-tradition? — hypotheses labeled as such; the text's facts (star, gifts, timing) argued, not the legends), and never claim Matthew INVENTED the star to fit Numbers (the magi-episode's embarrassments — pagan astrologers! astrology! — argue authenticity (criterion of embarrassment cuts for the church here).

Further Resources

  • Numbers 24 — Balaam oracles (BibleGateway)
  • Bar Kokhba revolt — archaeology/history (Britannica)

Q30Who is the 'prophet like Moses' — and does the description fit Muhammad?

Context

Deuteronomy 18:15-19 ('The LORD your God will raise up for you a prophet like me from among you, from your brothers') — with 34:10-12's epitaph ('no prophet has risen in Israel like Moses, whom the LORD knew face to face') — frames Israel's expectation: a Moses-grade mediator with signs, covenant-mediation, and divine converse. Three claimants: the prophetic succession generally (Joshua? — Jews: the verse founds ongoing prophecy, fulfilled across centuries); Muhammad (Islamic dawah: 'like Moses' — lawgiver! warrior! married! natural death! — versus Jesus' virgin birth/divinity making Him UNLIKE Moses (Deedat's argument!)); Jesus (Acts 3:22-23 — Peter; 7:37 — Stephen; John 1:45 — Philip: 'him of whom Moses wrote')). The 'brothers' clause decides half the debate before it starts.

Mainstream Position & Primary Sources

  • 'From among you, from your brothers' — Deuteronomy's own usage controls meaning: 17:15 (kings 'from among your brothers' — explicitly excluding foreigners: 'you may not put a foreigner over you, who is not your brother') proves 'brothers' = fellow Israelites. Muhammad (Ishmaelite, Arabian) is excluded by the Torah's own lexicon — the Islamic claim dies on the verse's fourth word. (Muslim rejoinder: Ishmaelites are Abrahamic 'brothers' broadly (Genesis 16:12; 25:18) — reply: Deuteronomy 17:15's restrictive use governs Deuteronomy 18's same author/context.)
  • Moses-likeness inventory (fair to all): lawgiver? (Moses: Torah; Muhammad: Sharia — point to Islam; Jesus: 'but I say to you' authoritative reinterpretation (Matthew 5) + new covenant (Luke 22:20) — point to Christ, differently); warrior? (Moses: yes; Muhammad: yes; Jesus: no — unless the likeness is mediatorial, not military); natural death? (Moses died; Muhammad died; Jesus died AND rose — exceeds, doesn't fail); face-to-face? (Moses: yes (Exodus 33:11); Muhammad: explicitly denied in Islam (7:143's vision-refusal pattern; Mi'raj's veil — Allah unseen!); Jesus: 'whoever has seen me has seen the Father' (John 14:9) + transfiguration (Moses present, deferring! — Matthew 17:3-5)); signs? (Moses: plagues/sea; Muhammad: Qur'an-only (Q21-entry!); Jesus: blind see, dead rise (Isaiah 35:5-6 checklist!)). Scoreboard: Muhammad 2/5, Jesus 5/5 (with resurrection bonus).
  • Samaritan expectation (Taheb — the Restorer-prophet) confirms the verse's eschatological charge in Second Temple Judaism (John 4:25 — Samaritan woman: 'Messiah is coming' from Torah-only canon! — Deuteronomy 18 working independently of Prophets!).

Primary Source References

  • Deuteronomy 18:15-19; 34:10-12; 17:15 (brothers-control).
  • Acts 3:22-23; 7:37; John 1:45; 4:25; 14:9.

Christian Apologetic Response

Prosecute 'brothers' first (Deuteronomy 17:15's exclusion of foreigners is the same book, same phrase, same Moses — the Islamic reading requires 'brothers' to mean opposite things three chapters apart; no competent exegete permits it). The Muhammad-claim fails at the threshold — everything after is surplus. THEN the likeness inventory, scored publicly (lawgiver/mediator/signs/face-to-face/death — present as a table in live debate; audiences track scoreboards): Muhammad's two points (law, death) are the generic ones (every founder legislates and dies); Jesus takes the specific ones (face-to-face converse — John 1:18's 'exegeted'; signs matching Isaiah's messianic checklist — Matthew 11:4-5's blind-lame-leper-deaf-dead-poor sequence is Isaiah 35 + 61 COMBINED — Jesus curating prophecy as His ID!). The inventory's shape favors the Christian even before resurrection is counted.

Close with the Samaritans (John 4's woman expecting Taheb from Deuteronomy alone!): the verse generated live messianic expectation among Torah-purists with no Prophets-canon — Jesus claims it to HER ('I who speak to you am he,' 4:26 — the gospel's most direct self-disclosure, to a Samaritan adulteress!). The prophet-like-Moses reveals Himself to outsiders while insiders debate — John's irony preaches. Ask Muslim claimants: did Muhammad ever claim Deuteronomy 18 for himself (he didn't — the claim is Deedat's, 14 centuries later!)? Self-claim matters (false prophets self-nominate; true ones are nominated by God — Hebrews 5:4!).

Points for Respectful Discussion

Credit Deedat's ingenuity (his Moses-parallel table converted thousands — understand its power before dismantling it), never mock Muhammad's illiteracy/militancy here (irrelevant to exegesis — the 'brothers' argument needs no biography), and present the scoreboard as joint Bible-study (Deuteronomy 17 controls 18 — let the partner verify in their own Tanakh; discovery persuades, assertion doesn't).

Q31Who sits on David's throne forever — and where is he?

Context

2 Samuel 7:12-16 (Nathan's oracle: David's offspring builds the house; 'I will establish the throne of his kingdom forever'; 'your house and kingdom shall be made sure forever') — the Davidic covenant, the Old Testament's political eschatology. History's verdict: no Davidide has reigned since Zedekiah (586 BCE) — 2,600 years of vacant throne (Persian governors, Hasmonean priests, Herodian Idumeans, then nothing). Jewish readings: conditional dynasty (Psalm 132:12 — 'if your sons keep my covenant'; exile suspended, restoration pending — Maimonides' human Messiah-king resumes it); the promise abides as future (Jeremiah 33:17 — 'David shall never lack a man'). Christian reading: Gabriel's annunciation IS the resumption notice (Luke 1:32-33 — 'throne of his father David... reign over Jacob forever, of his kingdom no end' — quoting 2 Samuel 7 verbatim!); the virginal conception solves the Jeconiah curse (Jeremiah 22:30 — no descendant of Jeconiah prospers on David's throne; Joseph descends from Jeconiah (Matthew 1:11-12!) — legal heir with cursed blood; Mary's line (Luke 3 — Nathan's branch, bypassing Jeconiah!) supplies uncursed blood; virgin birth unites legal right (adoption) with curse-evasion (no Jeconiah seed)!). Skeptics allege the genealogies contradict (Matthew vs. Luke) — the two-line solution (Joseph/Mary) answers precisely.

Mainstream Position & Primary Sources

  • The Jeconiah knot (under-appreciated, devastating to casual dismissal): Jeremiah 22:30 curses Jeconiah's seed from the throne; Matthew traces Jesus' LEGAL line through Jeconiah (Joseph) — if Jesus were Joseph's biological son, the curse would bar Him. The virgin birth isn't an awkward add-on but the curse's solution: legal heirship without cursed seed, uncursed blood without legal standing — both lines needed, both supplied. Either the evangelists engineered the most elegant legal-theological solution in antiquity, or history did it for them. (Objection: Luke's genealogy also hits Jeconiah? — no: Luke 3's line runs through Nathan, David's other son, bypassing Solomon's branch entirely. Objection: Mary in Luke 3? — 'son of Heli' via levirate/son-in-law convention (Heli as Mary's father, Joseph as son-in-law — ancient usage attested); even on worst reading, two independent Davidic lines converge.)
  • Vacant-throne arithmetic: 586 BCE → present = 26 centuries; Maimonides' Messiah must (a) be documented Davidide (tribal records perished in 70 — impossible now!), (b) rebuild Temple, (c) reign. The documentation problem alone forces a pre-70 Messiah (records existed then — Josephus/Hegesippus trace Davidides (Jesus' relatives!) into Domitian's reign!).

Primary Source References

  • 2 Samuel 7:12-16; Jeremiah 22:28-30; Psalm 132:11-12.
  • Matthew 1; Luke 1:32-33; 3:23-38; Acts 2:29-36.

Christian Apologetic Response

Present the Jeconiah solution slowly — it converts skeptics precisely because skeptics raised the problem (contradicting genealogies → complementary legal/biological lines; cursed heir → virgin bypass). The 'contradiction' is the proof's raw material: no fabricator invents a curse barring his hero then threads two genealogies through it. Then the vacancy arithmetic, pressed as a dilemma: the throne has sat empty 2,600 years; the covenant promised perpetuity; EITHER God failed (unthinkable to both parties) OR the perpetual King reigns non-territorially now (Acts 2:30-36 — raised to sit! — Peter's Pentecost logic: David's tomb occupied (v.29!), therefore the oath outruns David (v.30!), therefore resurrection-enthronement (vv.33-36!)). Peter argues from the same vacancy Jews lament — shared datum, apostolic conclusion. The empty throne is Christianity's exhibit A, not its embarrassment.

Add Hegesippus (Jesus' grandnephews hauled before Domitian as Davidides, examined, released as peasants — Eusebius 3.20!): David's line survived into the 90s CE — documented, harassed, poor. The identification-window was open in Jesus' generation and closed with the Temple's records. A Messiah must be identified Davidide; identification requires records; records died in 70. Therefore Messiah came before 70 — or never. The logic is remorseless; deliver it gently (it ends 2,000 years of waiting with arithmetic — grief precedes assent here).

Points for Respectful Discussion

Master both genealogies cold (names, branches, the Jeconiah junction — fumbling loses the5788778 room), concede the vacancy is genuinely tragic (2,600 years of promise-unkept appearance — lament with the partner before arguing; Psalm 89-entry next preaches the lament!), and never present the two-line solution as obvious (it took the church centuries to articulate — ancient difficulty honored, modern clarity offered).

  • Eusebius 3.20 — Domitian and David's kin (New Advent)

Q32Who is the Son in Psalm 2 — David, or someone greater?

Context

Psalm 2 (coronation liturgy? — nations raging, kings plotting 'against the LORD and against his Anointed,' the decree: 'You are my Son; today I have begotten you,' iron-rod rule, 'kiss the Son lest he be angry') — Davidic (Acts 4:25 attributes to David) yet overflowing David (ends-of-earth inheritance (v.8) — David never ruled past the Euphrates' bend; iron-shattering (v.9) — hyperbolic for any ancient king; 'kiss the Son' (v.12 — bar: 'son' (Aramaic loan?) vs. 'pure' (LXX?/Vulgate 'apprehend discipline'!) — textual crux!). Apostolic exegesis is unanimous and early: Acts 4:25-28 (the church's first prayer meeting applies vv.1-2 to Herod + Pilate + Gentiles + Israel conspiring against Jesus!), Acts 13:33 (resurrection as the 'today' of begetting!), Hebrews 1:5 (Sonship distinguishing Christ from angels!). Jewish reading: Davidic king generally (coronation hyperbole — ancient Near Eastern royal ideology routinely deifies kings verbally; Rashi: David; the 'son' adoptive (2 Samuel 7:14 — 'I will be to him a father')).

Mainstream Position & Primary Sources

  • The 'today I have begotten you' crux: adoptionist heretics (ancient and Jehovah's-Witness modern) read origin-in-time (Jesus BECAME Son at baptism/resurrection); orthodoxy reads eternal generation DECLARED in time (resurrection publishes the eternal relation — Romans 1:4!; the 'today' is the resurrection-day (Acts 13:33 explicit!)). Both sides agree the verse is temporally indexed; the debate is declaration versus constitution. (Islamic use (Q28-entry!): 'begotten' as physical — answered there: eternal generation, begotten-not-made (Nicaea!).)
  • 'Kiss the Son' philology (bar — Aramaism in Hebrew psalm? Ugaritic parallels? LXX 'draxasthe paideias' (seize instruction)!; Jerome's 'adorate pure'!; moderns divided): the Christian case doesn't need bar-as-son (v.7 already says 'my Son' unambiguously (beni attah!) — v.12's ambiguity can't sink v.7's clarity; argue from strength, concede the crux).
  • Acts 4's application (Peter's post-Pentecost prayer, weeks after the cross!): Herod (kings) + Pilate (rulers/Gentiles) + Israel (peoples) — the conspiracy's four parties mapped to the psalm's four rebels (nations/peoples/kings/rulers — vv.1-2!). Itemized fulfillment within a generation of composition's claim — either staged (conspiracy theorists' burden: who staged Rome?) or inspired.

Primary Source References

  • Psalm 2; 2 Samuel 7:14; Acts 4:25-28; 13:33; Hebrews 1:5.
  • Ancient Near Eastern royal ideology parallels (general knowledge).

Christian Apologetic Response

Argue Acts 4's itemization (the earliest Christian exegesis, pre-50 CE, praying not proving — worship-text, not proof-text!): four rebel-classes in the psalm, four conspirator-classes at the cross (Herod/Pilate/Gentiles/Israel — Luke's own categories (Luke 23:12 — Herod-Pilate friendship!; Acts 4:27 names all four!). Coincidence requires believing Jerusalem's power-structure accidentally quartet-matched a millennium-old poem on the exact weekend its King died. Then v.8's excess (ends of earth — David's empire: regional; Christ's: global (Gentile church — empirical!); v.9's shattering (Revelation 2:27 — risen Christ WIELDS the iron rod (quoting Psalm 2!) — the psalm's violence belongs to the returning Judge (Revelation 19:15!), not the bent David — eschatological reservation (Q2-framework!) handles the unfulfilled remainder without remainder.

On 'today begotten': press resurrection-publication (Acts 13:33's 'today' = Easter! — the begetting is eternal (John 1:14, 18 — monogenes!), the TODAY is manifestation (Romans 1:4 — 'declared Son... by resurrection'!). Easter doesn't MAKE Him Son; Easter ANNOUNCES Him (Romans 10:9's confession-content!). The Islamic begetting-objection (Q28) dissolves here too: eternal Son declared in time — no consort, no event, no biology (6:101 answered by eternity!). One exegesis answers synagogue, mosque, and cult simultaneously — preach it as such.

Points for Respectful Discussion

Concede bar's ambiguity upfront (lexicons genuinely divide — HALOT lists options; pretending certainty forfeits trust), anchor everything in v.7's unambiguous beni (no textual cloud there!), and present Acts 4 as prayer (the church SINGING Psalm 2 over persecution — exegesis as worship, the most credible kind). Never wield Psalm 2 as a threat ('kiss or perish' cudgeling) — the psalm ends in refuge-blessing (v.12 — 'blessed are all who take refuge' — GOSPEL ending!; threaten never, invite always).

Q33Whose body saw no corruption — David's, or another's?

Context

Psalm 16:10 ('you will not abandon my soul to Sheol, or let your holy one see corruption') — David's confidence-song (miktam; 'I have set the LORD always before me,' v.8; path-of-life joy, v.11) — became Pentecost's resurrection-proof (Acts 2:25-31) and Pisidian Antioch's (Acts 13:35-37) by one devastating observation: David died, was buried, and decayed (tomb known! — Acts 2:29: 'his tomb is with us to this day' — empirical, checkable, uncontested!). Peter's logic is a valid syllogism from shared premises: (1) David prophesied (v.10's speaker foresees); (2) David decayed (tomb!); (3) therefore David spoke of another (the Christ, v.31 — 'he foresaw and spoke about the resurrection'). Paul repeats it (Acts 13:36-37 — 'David... saw corruption, but he whom God raised up did not'). Jewish reading: Davidic confidence (preservation FROM death — God rescues the psalmist, as often; 'corruption' (shachat) as 'pit' (death), not decay — lexical debate!).

Mainstream Position & Primary Sources

  • Shachat crux (pit vs. corruption/decay): HALOT/BDB list both ('pit' (grave) and 'corruption' (decay)); LXX reads diaphthoran (corruption/decay — pre-Christian Jewish translation!); Aqulia/Symmachus later revise toward 'pit' (post-Christian Jewish revision?! — the revision-pattern itself evidences the debate (with Isaiah 7:14-entry's LXX/parthenos parallel — Jewish Greek Bibles keep embarrassing Christians' case until revised!). The Christian argument survives either reading: 'not abandoned to Sheol' + David's tomb-occupancy forces a beyond-David referent whether shachat means pit-permanence or decay (David stayed in Sheol's grip; the Holy One didn't).
  • Corporate-Israel reading (servant-pattern, with Isaiah 53-entry): nation preserved through exile — possible for some psalms, strained here (singular 'my flesh rests in hope' (v.9), 'your holy one' (hasidekha — singular devotee!) — the psalm's I-voice resists collectivizing; and Israel HAS seen corruption (Holocaust's pits — the collective reading breaks on history's worst datum).

Primary Source References

  • Psalm 16:8-11; Acts 2:25-32; 13:34-37.
  • LXX Psalm 15:10 (diaphthoran); David's tomb tradition (1 Kings 2:10).

Christian Apologetic Response

Peter's tomb-argument is the model for all prophecy-debate: shared datum (tomb occupied — no faith required to verify!), valid inference (prophet ≠ subject when subject falsifies predicate), apostolic conclusion (resurrection). Imitate the method everywhere (with Daniel-entry J6: shared decrees, computed dates; with Isaiah 53-entry: shared pronouns, pressed logic). The method IS the rebuttal to 'Christian spin' charges — no spin, just syllogism from Jewish premises (David's tomb + David's authorship + David's decay = another's resurrection). Ask the partner to fault a premise or grant the conclusion — tertium non datur (no third option!).

Then the LXX witness (diaphthoran — corruption — in the pre-Christian Jewish Bible!): Jews translating shachat as decay two centuries before Christ — the 'pit-only' reading is post-Christian revision (Aquila, c. 130 CE, translating FOR polemic (his renderings systematically de-christologize — virgin/young woman (Isaiah 7!), pit/corruption (here!), servant readings!). Document the revision-pattern (LXX vs. Aquila across messianic texts — consistent direction!) and ask what it proves: the pre-Christian Jewish Bible sounded Christian; post-Christian Judaism edited the sound out. Who's spinning whom? (Handle Aquila fairly — he was sincere; sincerity and motivated reasoning coexist (in us too — confess Christian motivated readings (Psalm 8 overreach?) to earn the charge.).

Points for Respectful Discussion

Visit David's tomb-tradition honestly (Mount Zion cenotaph — medieval tradition, actual location uncertain (City of David more likely!) — don't overclaim geography; the ARGUMENT needs only agreed decay (1 Kings 2:10 — 'David slept' + no resurrection-tradition for David anywhere in Judaism — conceded by all!). Concede shachat's range (pit AND corruption — lexicons list both; argue LXX-choice + tomb-logic, not lexical monopoly). Syllogism over semantics, always.

Q34Whose 'body was prepared' — and what does Hebrews do with Psalm 40?

Context

Psalm 40:6-8 ('Sacrifice and offering you have not desired, but you have given me an open ear... I delight to do your will... your law is within my heart') — thanksgiving liturgy (waiting, pit-rescue, new song — vv.1-3) pivoting to obedience-theology (the prophets' refrain: obedience over sacrifice — 1 Samuel 15:22; Isaiah 1:11; Hosea 6:6; Micah 6:6-8!). Hebrews 10:5-7 quotes it christologically with a textual twist: LXX's 'a body you have prepared for me' (soma katertiso moi) versus MT's 'ears you have dug for me' (oznayim karita li)! The variant must be disclosed, not hidden — credibility depends on it. Jewish reading: Davidic devotion (obedient ears, Torah internalized — the psalm's plain sense, beautiful and sufficient). Christian reading: the trajectory (sacrifice → obedience → obedient self-offering) terminates in incarnation (prepared body!) and Gethsemane ('not my will' — the delight-to-do-will perfected under ultimate cost).

Mainstream Position & Primary Sources

  • Textual honesty (non-negotiable): MT (ears) vs. LXX (body) — related images (dug ears → hearing → obedient body?) or divergent traditions (Hebrew vorlage differing? scribal?); Hebrews follows LXX (as often — 2/3 of NT citations match LXX against MT!); the argument's validity on MT-alone (obedience over sacrifice → who obeys perfectly? — the trajectory still runs to Christ (Philippians 2:8 — 'obedient to death'!)). Scholars divide (NT-use-of-OT literature: Beale, Moyise); the embarrassment (inspired author 'misquoting'?) dissolves in first-century citation-practice (LXX as Bible — Paul's Bible had 'body'!; inspiration accommodates versions (with qira'at-entry Islam Q33 — same version-plurality phenomenon, honestly parallel!).
  • Canonical trajectory (the real argument): sacrifice-critique WITHOUT abolition (prophets assume the cult continues — with atonement-entry J8!) creates eschatological pressure (who finally obeys?); the psalmist's 'I delight' (v.8) outruns every historical offerer (David's Bathsheba after Psalm 51's twin language! — the delight failed in the speaker!); Hebrews' solution (prepared body offered once (10:10!) — obedience incarnate, sacrificed) resolves the pressure the psalm creates. The logic works from MT (obedience-ideal) with LXX (body-means) as specification.

Primary Source References

  • Psalm 40:6-8; 1 Samuel 15:22; Hebrews 10:5-10.
  • LXX Psalm 39:7 (soma); Philippians 2:8.

Christian Apologetic Response

Disclose the variant FIRST ('your Bible says ears, mine says body — let's talk about why, because the answer strengthens the case'): the disclosure itself preaches (Christians needn't fear textual facts — our faith survived Westcott-Hort, Qumran, and Bart Ehrman; model fearlessness!). Then the trajectory-argument on shared MT ground (no LXX needed!): (1) God prefers obedience to sacrifice (conceded — prophets!); (2) no offerer obeys perfectly (David's fall post-psalm!; Israel's exile for disobedience!); (3) therefore the system awaits the Obedient One (the psalm's 'I delight' as promissory — delight unperformed by its singer!). Hebrews names Him (prepared body — LXX specifying MT's direction, not inventing it). The MT alone creates the vacancy; the LXX names the tenant; Easter proves the occupancy (resurrection as God's 'amen' to the offering (10:12-14 — 'sat down' — finished!). Vacancy → tenant → proof: three steps, each checkable.

Add the Davidic-embarrassment clincher (Bathsheba AFTER the delight-language (Psalm 51 reuses 40's idiom in repentance!): the psalmist who delighted-to-obey committed the Torah's showcase sins (adultery + murder, 2 Samuel 11-12!) — EITHER the psalm is aspirational fiction (unthinkable — it's canon!) OR it speaks beyond its singer (prophetic surplus — Peter's Psalm 16 logic (previous entry!) applied here: decayed singer → undecayed subject; failed obeyer → perfect Obeyer!). Same syllogism, new psalm — method consistency IS the cumulative case.

Points for Respectful Discussion

Quote the LXX/MT difference in full view (project both texts side by side in study — hiding it replicates the Aqulia-pattern (previous entry!) in reverse), grant inspiration-questions are genuinely hard (how God speaks through versions — 2 Timothy 3:16's graphe through LXX-graphe?! — theologians wrestle; admit mystery where mystery stands), and never cite Hebrews 10:5's 'body' without footnoting 'ears' (footnotes are credibility's currency — spend lavishly).
